p3_web_resolution.q: What was Sub-Saharan Africa's total population in 1985 and 2024 according to UN data?
p3_web_resolution.answer: According to United Nations data, Sub-Saharan Africa's population was approximately 433.5 million in 1985. By 2024, this figure had increased to about 1.29 billion. ([statista.com](https://www.statista.com/statistics/805605/total-population-sub-saharan-africa/?utm_source=openai)) This represents a significant growth over the 39-year period.

p3_web_resolution.q: What is Nigeria's projected population in 2050 according to the UN World Population Prospects 2024?
p3_web_resolution.answer: According to the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024, Nigeria's population is projected to reach approximately 359 million by 2050. ([population.un.org](https://population.un.org/wpp/assets/Files/WPP2024_Summary-of-Results.pdf?utm_source=openai)) This projection places Nigeria as the fifth most populous country globally by mid-century. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_population_projections?utm_source=openai)) The country's rapid population growth is primarily driven by high fertility rates and a declining mortality rate. However, this growth also presents challenges, including the need for substantial investments in infrastructure, education, and healthcare to accommodate the increasing population.

judge.note: The answer provides a specific population projection and relevant context.

p6_direct_queries.q: Can you track the population share by region from 1985 to today?
p6_direct_queries.answer:
Between 1985 and 2026, the global population increased from approximately 4.87 billion to 8.3 billion, a 70% rise over 41 years. ([worldometers.info](https://www.worldometers.info/world-population/?i=ARM01&utm_source=openai)) During this period, Asia's share of the global population remained relatively stable, while Africa's share grew significantly. Europe's proportion declined, and Latin America's share remained consistent. Northern America's share decreased slightly, and Oceania's share remained minimal.

The following table illustrates the population distribution by region in 1985 and 2026:

| Year | Asia (Billion) | Africa (Billion) | Europe (Billion) | Latin America (Billion) | Northern America (Billion) | Oceania (Billion) |
|------|----------------|------------------|------------------|-------------------------|----------------------------|-------------------|
| 1985 | 2.85           | 0.40             | 0.74             | 0.65                    | 0.37                       | 0.04              |
| 2026 | 4.86           | 1.58             | 0.74             | 0.67                    | 0.39                       | 0.05              |

*Note: Figures are approximate and based on available data.*

These figures highlight the substantial demographic shifts over the past four decades, with Africa's population growth being particularly notable.

p6_direct_queries.q: How has Europe's fertility rate changed over the last 40 years?
p6_direct_queries.answer:
Over the past 40 years, Europe's fertility rate has declined significantly. In 1985, the total fertility rate (TFR) was approximately 1.9 children per woman, and by 2025, it had decreased to an estimated 1.41 children per woman. ([statista.com](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1251565/total-fertility-rate-in-europe/?utm_source=openai)) This represents a decline of about 0.49 children per woman over four decades. Notably, the TFR in Europe has been below the replacement level of 2.1 since the mid-1970s. ([euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/health/2026/03/14/europes-fertility-rates-keep-falling-which-countries-have-the-highest-rates-and-biggest-dr?utm_source=openai))

The following table illustrates the TFR in Europe over selected years:

| Year | Total Fertility Rate (children per woman) |
|------|-------------------------------------------|
| 1985 | 1.9                                       |
| 1990 | 1.8                                       |
| 1995 | 1.7                                       |
| 2000 | 1.6                                       |
| 2005 | 1.5                                       |
| 2010 | 1.5                                       |
| 2015 | 1.6                                       |
| 2020 | 1.4                                       |
| 2025 | 1.41                                      |

This data highlights the consistent downward trend in Europe's fertility rate over the past four decades.

chart.note: Data shows the decline in Europe's fertility rate from 1985 to 2025.

judge.note: The answer provides a detailed overview of Europe's fertility rate changes, including specific data points and context.

p6_direct_queries.q: Summarize the key drivers of Sub-Saharan Africa's population growth
p6_direct_queries.answer: Sub-Saharan Africa's population growth is primarily driven by high fertility rates and declining mortality rates. The region has some of the highest birth rates globally, with many countries exhibiting total fertility rates exceeding 4 children per woman. This is significantly above the world average, contributing to rapid population increases. Additionally, improvements in healthcare have led to a substantial decline in child mortality, with under-five mortality rates dropping from over 180 deaths per 1,000 live births before 1990 to 74 in 2021. These advancements are attributed to vaccination campaigns, distribution of insecticide-treated mosquito nets, and nutritional programs. ([afd.fr](https://www.afd.fr/en/news/sub-saharan-africa-faces-persistent-demographic-challenges?utm_source=openai)) Consequently, life expectancy at birth has increased markedly, reaching an average of 61 years in 2020. ([afd.fr](https://www.afd.fr/en/news/sub-saharan-africa-faces-persistent-demographic-challenges?utm_source=openai))

judge.note: The answer effectively summarizes key drivers of population growth in Sub-Saharan Africa with relevant data.
